lit: alarming words that make the listener start in fright

use.how: Predicate or after 是/不是, about what someone says or writes to scare people: 这不是危言耸听。 Often used to insist a warning is real.

near.diff: 杞人忧天 is worrying yourself about imaginary dangers; 危言耸听 is saying alarming things to frighten others.
大惊小怪 is overreacting to something ordinary; 危言耸听 is exaggerating a danger in words to alarm an audience.

cue: A doctor warns that staying up every night really can damage your heart, and adds that she is not just trying to scare you.

ctx.s: 我说的都是真的，绝对不是{危言耸听}。
ctx.en: Everything I said is true; I'm absolutely not just trying to scare you.

ctx.s: 有些自媒体为了流量，故意{危言耸听}。
ctx.en: Some self-media accounts deliberately spread alarmist talk to get clicks.

ctx.s: 专家说这种说法纯属{危言耸听}，大家不必恐慌。
ctx.en: Experts say the claim is pure scaremongering and there is no need to panic.

ctx.s: “再不保护环境，后果不堪设想。”“你这是不是有点{危言耸听}了？”
ctx.en: "If we don't protect the environment, the consequences will be unthinkable." "Aren't you being a bit alarmist?"

ctx.s: 他的报告并非{危言耸听}，每个数字都有出处。
ctx.en: His report is not scaremongering; every figure has a source.

ctx.s: 那些{危言耸听}的保健广告，让不少老人花了冤枉钱。
ctx.en: Those alarmist health-product ads have made many elderly people waste their money.

bad.s: 老师的讲课很{危言耸听}，同学们都爱听。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher's lectures are gripping and everyone loves them)
bad.why: It is a criticism of scaring people with exaggerated warnings, not praise for exciting or captivating speech.

bad.s: 我一个人在家，越想越{危言耸听}，睡不着觉。
bad.en: (meant: alone at home, the more I thought the more frightened I got)
bad.why: It describes words said to alarm others, not a person's own feeling of fear.

lit: to shift hidden from view and change in silence

story.text: In his family instructions, the sixth-century scholar Yan Zhitui warns his sons to choose their companions with care. A young person's character is not yet settled, he says; spending time with someone, laughing and talking with them, you take on their ways without meaning to learn anything, changing unnoticed until you naturally resemble them. His wording differs by one character from the idiom used today.

use.how: Adverbial with 地 before 影响/改变, or as the attributive 潜移默化的影响/作用. Said of slow influence from environment, people or culture.

near.diff: 耳濡目染 stresses picking something up by constantly seeing and hearing it; 潜移默化 stresses that the change happens unnoticed, and can describe the influence itself.

cue: No one ever lectured her, but after years in a tidy dorm she gradually became tidy herself, without noticing when it happened.

ctx.s: 好的环境会{潜移默化}地影响孩子。
ctx.en: A good environment influences children gradually without their noticing.

ctx.s: 音乐对人的情绪有一种{潜移默化}的作用。
ctx.en: Music has a subtle, gradual effect on people's moods.

ctx.s: 他口音的变化是{潜移默化}的，连他自己都没有察觉。
ctx.en: The change in his accent happened so gradually that even he didn't notice it.

ctx.s: 父母的一言一行，都在{潜移默化}地塑造着孩子的性格。
ctx.en: Everything parents say and do is quietly shaping their child's character.

ctx.s: 你没发现吗？广告正在{潜移默化}地改变我们的消费习惯。
ctx.en: Haven't you noticed? Advertising is quietly changing our spending habits.

ctx.s: 传统文化的教育重在{潜移默化}，而不是死记硬背。
ctx.en: Teaching traditional culture relies on gradual influence, not rote memorisation.

bad.s: 他昨天突然{潜移默化}，变成了另一个人。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday he suddenly changed into a different person)
bad.why: The idiom means slow, unnoticed change over a long time; it cannot describe a sudden change.

bad.s: 我每天{潜移默化}地背五十个单词。
bad.en: (meant: I deliberately memorise fifty words every day)
bad.why: It is influence absorbed without effort or intent, not deliberate study done on purpose.

lit: the roots are deep and the base of the fruit stalk is firm

story.text: The Daodejing speaks of the way to govern a state and keep it long: hold back and conserve, and you build up virtue. This, it says, is called making the roots deep and the base firm, the way of long life and lasting vision. The original has the two halves in a different order and spelling; later writers turned the image into this fixed phrase.

use.how: Predicate or attributive, mostly about ideas, habits, prejudices or traditions: 这种观念根深蒂固. Usually about something one wishes would change.

near.diff: 习以为常 is getting used to something until it seems normal; 根深蒂固 says a belief or habit is so entrenched it resists change.

cue: Laws now treat sons and daughters equally, yet in some villages people still believe a family must have a son, and this view will not budge.

ctx.s: 这种老观念在他心里{根深蒂固}。
ctx.en: This old idea is deeply rooted in his mind.

ctx.s: 要改变{根深蒂固}的偏见，需要很长时间。
ctx.en: Changing deep-rooted prejudices takes a long time.

ctx.s: “重男轻女”的思想在一些地方依然{根深蒂固}。
ctx.en: The idea of valuing sons over daughters is still entrenched in some places.

ctx.s: 他晚睡的习惯已经{根深蒂固}，怎么劝都没用。
ctx.en: His habit of going to bed late is so ingrained that no amount of persuasion helps.

ctx.s: 为什么这些错误的说法会如此{根深蒂固}呢？
ctx.en: Why are these mistaken claims so firmly rooted?

ctx.s: 公司里{根深蒂固}的官僚作风，让新经理很头疼。
ctx.en: The entrenched bureaucratic style in the company gives the new manager a headache.

bad.s: 这棵小树刚种下，就已经{根深蒂固}了。
bad.en: (meant: the sapling has just been planted and its roots are already deep)
bad.why: It is figurative, used for ideas and habits; describing a real young tree this way is wrong, and 'just planted' contradicts 'deep'.

bad.s: 我对这个城市的印象{根深蒂固}，因为我昨天才来。
bad.en: (meant: my impression of the city is strong, because I only arrived yesterday)
bad.why: It needs something built up over a long time; a one-day-old impression cannot be deep-rooted.

mean: so used to it that it seems normal
lit: through habit, to take it as ordinary

use.how: Predicate, often with 早已/已经, or in 对……习以为常. Said of something once surprising or hard that has become routine.

near.diff: 根深蒂固 is an entrenched belief or habit that resists change; 习以为常 is no longer noticing or minding something because it happens so often.

cue: When she first moved to the city the subway crowds shocked her; three years on, being squeezed in every morning no longer bothers her at all.

ctx.s: 他每天加班，家人早已{习以为常}。
ctx.en: He works overtime every day, and his family has long since got used to it.

ctx.s: 刚来时觉得这里太吵，现在已经{习以为常}了。
ctx.en: When I first came I thought it was too noisy here; now I'm used to it.

ctx.s: 对这种小事，大家都{习以为常}，没人在意。
ctx.en: Everyone is so used to such little things that no one cares.

ctx.s: 难道我们要对浪费粮食{习以为常}吗？
ctx.en: Are we really going to accept wasting food as normal?

ctx.s: 刚搬来时她很怕停电，住了半年也就{习以为常}了。
ctx.en: When she first moved there she dreaded the power cuts, but after half a year she got used to them.

ctx.s: “你不觉得冷吗？”“在东北长大，零下二十度我早就{习以为常}了。”
ctx.en: "Aren't you cold?" "I grew up in the Northeast; twenty below has long been normal for me."

bad.s: 他第一次坐飞机，就{习以为常}了。
bad.en: (meant: he took his first flight and found it normal)
bad.why: It needs repeated experience over time; nothing becomes habitual on the very first try.

bad.s: 我{习以为常}每天早上六点起床。
bad.en: (meant: I am in the habit of getting up at six every day)
bad.why: It does not take an object; use a plain verb meaning to be accustomed to, or put the thing before it.

lit: the ears are soaked and the eyes are dyed

use.how: Adverbial clause, often 从小耳濡目染, followed by what was learned. Said of skills, tastes or habits picked up from one's surroundings.

near.diff: 潜移默化 stresses unnoticed change and can name the influence itself; 耳濡目染 stresses learning by constantly seeing and hearing, usually from childhood.

cue: Her parents ran a tea shop, and by watching and listening to them every day as a child she can tell good tea from bad without ever being taught.

ctx.s: 他爸爸是厨师，他从小{耳濡目染}，也会做菜。
ctx.en: His father is a chef; having watched him since childhood, he can cook too.

ctx.s: 爷爷天天听京剧，她{耳濡目染}，也成了小戏迷。
ctx.en: Her grandfather listened to Peking opera every day; hearing it all around her, she became a little fan too.

ctx.s: 孩子在父母天天吵架的家里{耳濡目染}，脾气也变得急躁。
ctx.en: Growing up in a home where his parents quarrelled every day, the child absorbed it and became short-tempered too.

ctx.s: 你没学过法律，怎么这么懂？是在家里{耳濡目染}的吧？
ctx.en: You never studied law, so how do you know so much? You must have picked it up at home.

ctx.s: 在茶乡长大的人，{耳濡目染}，个个都懂点茶。
ctx.en: People who grow up in tea country pick it up around them; every one knows something about tea.

ctx.s: 作家在书中回忆，正是童年的{耳濡目染}让他走上了写作之路。
ctx.en: The writer recalls in his book that it was what he absorbed as a child that set him on the path of writing.

bad.s: 我昨天在网上{耳濡目染}了一节语法课。
bad.en: (meant: I watched a grammar lesson online yesterday)
bad.why: It means absorbing something from long, constant exposure, not attending a single lesson; and it takes no object.

bad.s: 我很努力地{耳濡目染}，终于考上了大学。
bad.en: (meant: I studied hard and got into university)
bad.why: It describes learning that happens effortlessly from surroundings, not hard deliberate study.

mean: to be together day in, day out
lit: to be with each other morning and evening

use.how: Predicate or attributive (朝夕相处的同事), about people who live, work or study together for a long period.

near.diff: 形影不离 means always going everywhere together, a sign of closeness; 朝夕相处 just means sharing daily life over time, as roommates or colleagues do.

cue: After four years sharing a dorm room, eating and studying side by side every day, two classmates have to say goodbye at graduation.

ctx.s: 我们在一个宿舍{朝夕相处}了四年。
ctx.en: We lived together in the same dorm, day in, day out, for four years.

ctx.s: 和{朝夕相处}的同事告别，心里很难受。
ctx.en: Saying goodbye to colleagues I saw every day was really hard.

ctx.s: {朝夕相处}久了，难免会有些小矛盾。
ctx.en: When you're together every day for a long time, small conflicts are inevitable.

ctx.s: 在训练营里，队员们{朝夕相处}，感情越来越深。
ctx.en: At the training camp, the team members spent every day together and grew ever closer.

ctx.s: 你跟他{朝夕相处}，怎么会不知道他生病了？
ctx.en: You're with him every single day; how could you not know he was ill?

ctx.s: 多年{朝夕相处}，这条老狗早已成了家里的一员。
ctx.en: After years of sharing our daily lives, the old dog has long since become one of the family.

bad.s: 我们在火车上{朝夕相处}了半个小时。
bad.en: (meant: we sat together on the train for half an hour)
bad.why: It means sharing daily life over a long time; half an hour together is far too short.

bad.s: 我每个月和他{朝夕相处}一次。
bad.en: (meant: I meet up with him once a month)
bad.why: Morning and evening means every day; occasional meetings contradict the idiom.

lit: in a hurry to seek success

use.how: Predicate, often in advice: 不要急于求成, 学习不能急于求成. Criticises impatience for results in study, work or reform.

near.diff: 拔苗助长 is the harmful action of forcing growth and spoiling it; 急于求成 is the impatient attitude that may lead to it.
一蹴而就 says something gets done in one go (usually that it can't); 急于求成 criticises the person who wants quick results.

cue: A beginner at the gym tells his coach he wants a six-pack within two weeks and plans to train four hours a day.

ctx.s: 学外语要慢慢来，不能{急于求成}。
ctx.en: Learning a foreign language takes time; you can't expect quick results.

ctx.s: 他太{急于求成}，结果练得受了伤。
ctx.en: He was too impatient for results and ended up injuring himself in training.

ctx.s: “我想一个月就减十公斤。”“别{急于求成}，对身体不好。”
ctx.en: "I want to lose ten kilos in a month." "Don't rush it, it's bad for your health."

ctx.s: 很多创业者失败，就是因为{急于求成}。
ctx.en: Many entrepreneurs fail precisely because they want results too fast.

ctx.s: 改革需要耐心，{急于求成}只会适得其反。
ctx.en: Reform requires patience; rushing for results will only backfire.

ctx.s: 你是不是有点{急于求成}了？才练了三天就想上台演出。
ctx.en: Aren't you rushing things a bit? You've practised for three days and already want to perform on stage.

bad.s: 他{急于求成}，很快就完成了任务，老板很满意。
bad.en: (meant: he worked fast, finished the task quickly and the boss was pleased)
bad.why: It is criticism of impatience, not praise for working efficiently.

bad.s: 火车快开了，我{急于求成}地跑向站台。
bad.en: (meant: the train was about to leave, so I hurried to the platform)
bad.why: It means being impatient for results in a long task, not physically hurrying to catch something.

lit: duty does not allow one to decline

use.how: Predicate or in 义不容辞的责任/义务, usually said by someone accepting a task as their duty: 这是我义不容辞的责任。

cue: Asked whether he'd mind helping evacuate flood victims from his own village, a young soldier says it is simply his duty and of course he'll go.

ctx.s: 帮助有困难的同学，是我们{义不容辞}的事。
ctx.en: Helping classmates in difficulty is something we can't refuse to do.

ctx.s: 家乡有难，我{义不容辞}，第一个报名当志愿者。
ctx.en: My hometown is in trouble; it's my duty, so I was the first to sign up as a volunteer.

ctx.s: 保护孩子的安全，是学校{义不容辞}的责任。
ctx.en: Keeping children safe is the school's bounden duty.

ctx.s: “这次救灾你愿意去吗？”“当然，{义不容辞}！”
ctx.en: "Are you willing to join the disaster relief this time?" "Of course, it's my duty!"

ctx.s: 作为医生，抢救病人是{义不容辞}的义务。
ctx.en: As a doctor, saving patients is an obligation you cannot refuse.

ctx.s: 老同学请他做婚礼证婚人，他觉得{义不容辞}，一口答应了。
ctx.en: When an old classmate asked him to officiate at the wedding, he felt it was his duty and agreed at once.

bad.s: 他请我吃饭，我{义不容辞}地拒绝了。
bad.en: (meant: he invited me to dinner and I firmly refused)
bad.why: It means one cannot refuse a duty; it cannot describe refusing anything, and a dinner invitation is not a duty.

bad.s: 老板让我加班，我{义不容辞}这个任务。
bad.en: (meant: the boss asked me to work late and I accepted the task)
bad.why: It takes no object, and it is for a moral duty, not routine overtime ordered by a boss.

mean: wishing to help but unable to
lit: loving him, yet no one can help

story.text: An ode in the Book of Songs praises Zhong Shanfu, a minister of King Xuan of Zhou. It says that virtue is light as a hair, yet few people can lift it; only Zhong Shanfu lifts it. The poet loves him for it but no one can help him. Its wording lacks one character of the idiom; from it comes the idiom, now said when you sympathise but cannot help.

use.how: Predicate, usually said by the speaker about themselves to decline politely: 这件事我爱莫能助。 Often with 实在, 只能.

near.diff: 无能为力 is plain powerlessness, about anything; 爱莫能助 adds that you sympathise and would like to help someone.
力不从心 is your ability failing your own aims; 爱莫能助 is being unable to help another person.

cue: A friend asks you to get her son into your company, but hiring is not your decision, and you tell her, sorry, much as you'd like to, you can't.

ctx.s: 不是我不想帮你，这件事我实在{爱莫能助}。
ctx.en: It's not that I don't want to help; there's really nothing I can do about this.

ctx.s: 他想借钱，可我自己也没钱，只能{爱莫能助}。
ctx.en: He wanted to borrow money, but I'm broke myself, so I can only say I'm sorry I can't help.

ctx.s: “你能帮我改一下成绩吗？”“这不合规定，我{爱莫能助}。”
ctx.en: "Could you change my grade?" "That's against the rules; sorry, I can't help with that."

ctx.s: 我很同情他的遭遇，也很想拉他一把，可惜{爱莫能助}。
ctx.en: I feel for him and would love to give him a hand, but sadly I can't help.

ctx.s: 签证的事归大使馆管，我们学校也{爱莫能助}。
ctx.en: Visas are up to the embassy; much as we sympathise, our school can't help.

ctx.s: 他写信向老同学求助，对方回信说{爱莫能助}。
ctx.en: He wrote to an old classmate for help, and the reply said he regretted he could not help.

bad.s: 他病得很重，医生{爱莫能助}地治好了他。
bad.en: (meant: the doctor helped and cured him)
bad.why: It means one cannot help; it cannot go with actually helping or succeeding.

bad.s: 我自己做作业时，这道数学题太难，我{爱莫能助}。
bad.en: (meant: doing my own homework, this maths problem was too hard for me)
bad.why: It is about being unable to help another person; for your own inability say you cannot solve it.

mean: one's ability falls short of one's wishes
lit: strength does not follow the heart

use.how: Predicate, often with 感到/有些/越来越: 感到力不从心. Said of oneself or another, often because of age, illness or too much work.

near.diff: 爱莫能助 is being unable to help someone else; 力不从心 is your own strength or ability not matching what you want to do.
无能为力 says nothing can be done at all; 力不从心 says you want to and partly try, but your strength falls short.

cue: Your grandmother still wants to tend her big vegetable garden, but at eighty-five her back can no longer manage the digging she loves.

ctx.s: 爷爷年纪大了，爬山时常常{力不从心}。
ctx.en: Grandpa is getting old; when he climbs hills, his body often can't do what he wants.

ctx.s: 一个人管三个部门，她越来越感到{力不从心}。
ctx.en: Managing three departments alone, she feels more and more that she can't cope.

ctx.s: 病好以后他想马上恢复跑步，可还是有些{力不从心}。
ctx.en: After recovering he wanted to start running again right away, but his body still couldn't quite manage it.

ctx.s: 老队长说，每天带队训练，他已经{力不从心}了。
ctx.en: The old captain said that leading training every day was now beyond his strength.

ctx.s: 你是不是觉得工作量太大，有些{力不从心}？
ctx.en: Do you feel the workload is too much and you're struggling to keep up?

ctx.s: 这家小公司想跟大企业竞争，难免{力不从心}。
ctx.en: This small company wants to compete with big firms, so it's bound to find itself out of its depth.

bad.s: 他不想学习，所以考试{力不从心}。
bad.en: (meant: he didn't want to study, so he did badly in the exam)
bad.why: It requires wanting to do something but lacking the ability; with no wish to do it, the idiom does not fit.

bad.s: 他力气很大，一个人就{力不从心}地把箱子搬上楼了。
bad.en: (meant: he is strong and carried the box upstairs effortlessly)
bad.why: It means strength falls short; it cannot describe managing something easily.
